glossary.meaning: The four steps this tool follows: 1.0 Registration, 2.0 Assessment of submitted documents, 3.0 Validation (testing), 4.0 Issuance of certificate.
The vendor or in-house developer that applies to have its EMR system validated.
The company (third-party EMR provider) or the facility's own IT team (in-house developer) that builds and maintains the EMR system.
Applicant categories: a commercial product offered to many facilities, or a system developed by or for one facility / LGU.
The team that conducts the evaluation: 1 Technical Lead, 2 to 3 Validators, 1 Administrator and 1 to 2 Observers. Recorded in System Profile section C.
Supervises the evaluation, decides on equivalent controls, and approves the validation results and the conformance decision.
Conducts the testing using the Validator's Guide, records results and evidence references, re-tests corrected items and recommends approval.
Processes the application, assigns the Application No., keeps the logbook and evidence repository, schedules sessions, invites Observers and facilitates signing of the certificate.
A representative of an LGU, hospital, academic or research institution or other agency who witnesses the validation to ensure unbiased processing. Observers do not score.
The DOH office or region that conducts the validation (System Profile C.14); printed on the report letterhead and named in the statement of the certificate.
The reference number the Administrator assigns when the application is registered (System Profile A.0).
The signed letter by which the vendor formally applies for validation (L0-01).
The officer allowed to sign for the company, shown by a document such as a secretary's certificate, board resolution or office order.
A signed promise by the vendor — here, to follow the IGs, to be re-tested after changes, and to use only test data (L0-04).
A signed statement by an authorized officer that something is true (e.g., that backups are encrypted), accepted as evidence when the full document is confidential.
A signed promise by the Regional Validation Team to use the vendor's evidence only for this validation and keep it private.
The first meeting between the vendor's contact persons and the Regional Validation Team before testing (L0-05).
The signature section of the Printed Evaluation Report; names come from System Profile section C.
Signature of the vendor's authorized signatory acknowledging the evaluation result.

The document issued after approval stating that a specific product version was validated, with its Level 2 to 4 results and the versions it was validated against. Printed from Output › Certificate on one A4 page (landscape or portrait). PROOF OF CONCEPT: the design and process in this tool are for discussion and do not represent the actual DOH certificate (Chapter 7.4).

A 16-character code (first 16 hexadecimal digits of SHA-256) computed from the certificate's details, its FHIR release and its Level 2 to 4 results. Printed beside the security emblem; any change to a printed detail gives a different fingerprint. It is not a signature: anyone can compute it, so authenticity comes from the register of issued certificates (Chapter 7.6).

The list of every issued certificate, kept in criteria/certificates-issued.yaml and changed only by reviewed commits. A certificate counts as issued only once its entry is recorded; the Verify page answers from it. Each entry also keeps the validation record (Chapter 7.8).

The part of a register entry that keeps the full result of the validation: evaluation details, the status of each level and, for every sheet, the score, pass mark, status, criterion counts and the criteria still needing compliance. Not printed; shown on the Verify page (Chapter 7.8).
The round mark at the foot of the certificate: the QR code in front and the security rosette behind it, both drawn from the certificate fingerprint (Chapter 7.6).

The pattern behind and around the QR code: a ring of 64 long and short ticks that spells the fingerprint, a guilloche ring with 6 to 14 lobes, and faint slanted lines behind the code. Each certificate has its own; the Verify page redraws it for comparison with the paper (Chapter 7.6).
The 64 radial ticks around the security emblem, read clockwise from the ▼ mark: a long tick is a 1 and a short tick a 0 of the certificate fingerprint's 64 bits.

Fine, interlaced line patterns (the border band, the corner rosettes and the ring of the security emblem) that are hard to redraw by hand and blur when copied. On the certificate they are drawn from the certificate fingerprint.
Very small repeated text along the frame of the certificate, including the certificate number. Readable with a magnifier on the original; it blurs on photocopies and scans.
How much of a QR code can be damaged and still read: L about 7 %, M 15 %, Q 25 %. The certificate uses level L, the smallest code for its address, so each module prints large (Chapter 7.6).

Output › Verify a certificate: answers from the register of issued certificates whether a certificate is Valid, Expired, Superseded, Revoked or Not found, shows its details and validation record, and redraws its security emblem (Chapter 7.7).
A certificate printed while an item is still open (a detail missing, levels not passed, thresholds not approved, or a criteria version not released). It carries SPECIMEN — NOT VALID across the page.

The certificate printed again from its register entry on the Verify page, with the same fingerprint and security emblem. Marked as a copy: not valid without the signature of the signatory and the official seal (Chapter 7.7).
A fictional entry in the register of issued certificates (marked sample) for reviewers to try the Verify page and the register copy. It was never issued (Chapter 7.9).
A certificate replaced by a later one, recorded with supersedes: <old number> in the new entry; the Verify page then answers Superseded for the old number.
The officer who signs the certificate: the Head of KMITS or the DOH CHD Regional Director (System Profile, Certificate section).
Meeting the rules of the standard. A system is conformant for use in the HIE when Levels 0 to 3 are PASSED and no critical item is Not Met.
Repeating the validation (fully or partly) after a new major release, a change in the IGs, or another trigger in Chapter 7.
Retest: testing a failed item again after the vendor corrects it. Regression test: re-testing related items to make sure a change did not break them; needed when the build changes.
Where the system runs: on an internet provider's servers (cloud), on the facility's own servers (on-premise), or both (hybrid).
How long a certificate remains valid before revalidation is due (proposed: 2 years or until a major change / IG major version).
A release is a published version of the software; the version or build number identifies exactly which code was tested (System Profile A.3 and D.1).
The vendor's list of what changed in a version (L1-06).
Change classes that decide whether a new version needs full revalidation, partial regression testing or only a notice (Chapter 7).
The time allowed for certified systems to adopt a new IG version before revalidation is due (proposed: 6 months).
Spot checks of a certified system in production to confirm it still conforms.
Temporary (suspension) or permanent (revocation) withdrawal of a certificate for the reasons listed in Chapter 7.
A threshold, default or rule drafted in this tool that takes effect only after DOH approval is recorded on the Summary sheet.
A conformance result shown while the pass thresholds are still PROPOSED.
A value (e.g., idle time-out of 15 minutes) set by the DOH before evaluation and applied equally to all systems; may be adjusted only by the DOH.
A different security measure the vendor considers equal to or stronger than the Technical Baseline; accepted only if the Technical Lead approves it before testing.
An interoperability testing event where vendors exchange data with each other; items tagged "(Connectathon Issue #n)" come from the June 2026 PHeReF Connectathon issue log.
One of five gated stages (0 to 4). Each must be PASSED before the next counts.
A level or part that must be passed before the next one counts. TS0 is the gate inside Level 2.
The four sub-sections of Level 2: 2A TS0 Terminology & Registries, 2B TS1 Submission, 2C TS2 Retrieval, 2D Security, Reliability & Exception Handling.
A scripted test performed on the sandbox: TS0 terminology, TS1 submission, TS2 retrieval, TS3 exception (error-path) scenarios. Not a real-world use of the EMR.
Prefix of the TECHNICAL security and reliability criteria in Level 2D (TEC-01 to TEC-14), e.g., encryption, accounts, roles, audit log, backup.

The error-path tests in Level 2D (TS3-01 to TS3-09): missing or malformed data, invalid references, duplicate submission, interruption and retry, partial failure, service outage, credential failure, receiving-side outage.
Level 4 tags. Core-track items are fundamental and will move to Level 2 when the IG models them; Maturity items stay optional targets.
One requirement row with its own ID (e.g., TS1-04). IDs are never renumbered or reused.
One countable part of a Count criterion, with its own ID (e.g., TS1-04.2).
A criterion that must be Met for the level to pass, whatever the score.

A sub-item that must be Met; if it is Not Met or N/A the whole criterion counts as a critical failure, although other sub-items still give partial credit. Shown as "★ subs" in the Critical column of the parent.
Met = 100%, Not Met = 0%.
Partial credit: score = sub-items Met ÷ applicable sub-items (e.g., 8 of 10 = 80%).
Marked like Count, but 100% only when every sub-item is Met; otherwise 0%.
Used only for L1-04: Fully integrated = 100%; Standalone – manual encoding = 50%; Not Met = 0%.
Fully integrated: patient details already in the EMR reach the referral without re-typing. Standalone – manual encoding: some details must be typed again.
An item recorded for information, with weight 0, that does not affect the score.
How much a criterion counts in the score: critical items 2, others 1, information-only 0.
For Count criteria: number of applicable sub-items / number Met (calculated).
The evaluator's choice for a row (Met, Not Met, Not Tested, N/A, or the Tier level); for Count criteria it is calculated ("Counted").
Not yet evaluated; scores 0% and makes the sheet INCOMPLETE.
Removes a non-critical item from the score; on a critical item it counts as Not Met. The reason must be written in Notes.
The column that lists automatically which sub-items still need compliance.
A criterion or sub-item that is Not Met or only partly met; listed automatically in report section D.
The minimum level score needed to pass (Summary column D).
Sheet and level statuses: all tested, critical items Met and threshold reached / a condition failed / some items Not Tested / previous level not yet passed.
Share of items already evaluated (not the score).
The live table on the Summary sheet that counts criteria, critical items and sub-items per part; quote these figures in presentations.
For each row: what the vendor must prepare or implement / the steps the Validators follow to verify it.
What a result is based on, written in the Notes column: file or screenshot name, SHR resource ID and version, IOL transaction ID.
The ways a vendor may prove a confidential design: full document, redacted copy plus signed attestation, independent certification, or view-only presentation.
With confidential parts blacked out or removed.
The vendor shows a document on screen without handing it over; the Validator records it as "sighted".
Verification done on the Shared Health Record, not on the EMR screen, using one of: the Interoperability Layer log, a validator / Inferno report, or the raw request and response payload.
Testing by using the system as a user would, without seeing its source code or internals.
A criterion states WHAT must be achieved, not HOW; the vendor's technology choices are never scored.
The fictional values and expected results in the Test Data sheet: Section A test referral, Section B 10 known referrals, Section C Level 3 edge cases, Section D error inputs.
Known test referrals whose expected report values are calculated in advance; reconciliation means checking that the system's reports equal those values.
An unusual but valid situation (e.g., a referral at 23:50 on the last day of a month) used to check that rules hold at the limits.
Test records the DOH places on the SHR in advance with fixed timestamps (Test Data Section C).
A value in brackets in the Test Data that must be replaced with the official dummy value issued by the DOH.
Made-up test values that do not belong to any real person or facility.
The A4 report sheet that collects all results automatically for printing and signing; it has no input cells.
The heading at the top of each report page (Republic of the Philippines · Department of Health · conducting office).
A criterion ID no longer used on its sheet; it is never reused (list in section 2.12).
Sending a patient referral from one facility to another electronically through the HIE instead of on paper.

glossary.meaning: The ability of different systems to exchange data and use it correctly without re-typing.
The network through which facilities exchange patient and referral data using the national FHIR standards via the Shared Health Record.
The central FHIR server where referrals and related records are stored and from which receiving facilities retrieve them.
The middleware between the EMRs and the SHR that routes, authenticates and logs every transaction (e.g., OpenHIM).
Open Health Information Mediator — open-source interoperability-layer software that keeps a log of each transaction.
The DOH test servers used for validation; only fictional data is used there.
The internet address of a server or service the EMR connects to.
A defined way for one system to request data or actions from another.
Health Level Seven International — the organisation that publishes health data standards, including FHIR.
Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources — the HL7 standard for exchanging health data as "resources" over the web.
Release 4 of FHIR, the version required by Technical Baseline TB-10.
A published set of FHIR rules for a country or use case.
The Philippine base FHIR rules: patient, practitioner, organization, identifiers, addresses, etc.
The Philippine eReferral FHIR rules built on PH Core: referral request, task, clinical content, value sets.
Technical Design Group / Clinical Design Group of the PHeReF IG project, which maintain the technical mappings and clinical content.
University of the Philippines Manila — National Telehealth Center, which hosts the PH Core and PHeReF IG source (GitHub) and the SNOMED CT National Release Center.
One type of FHIR record, such as Patient or ServiceRequest. Each stored resource has a resource ID.
The server's identifier of a stored resource, and its version number (meta.versionId); old versions can be read through _history.
A profile constrains a FHIR resource for local use (which elements are required, which codes are allowed); it is published as a StructureDefinition.
The element in which a resource declares which profile it follows (TS1-T.03).
The permanent web address that identifies a profile, value set or code system (e.g., https://fhir.doh.gov.ph/pheref/StructureDefinition/ereferral-task).
The fully expanded form of a profile showing every element with its final rules; used to build the FHIR Traceability table.
One field inside a resource, written as Resource.element (e.g., Patient.birthDate).
How many times an element may or must appear: minimum..maximum. 1..1 = exactly once (mandatory); 0..* = optional, repeating.
An element with minimum cardinality 1; a resource without it is invalid.
An IG flag: the sender must send the element when the data exists and the receiver must be able to use it.
A named sub-type of a repeating element in a profile (e.g., PHCorePhilSysID and PHCorePhilHealthID of Patient.identifier; NhfrCode of Organization.identifier).
An extra element defined by an IG for data the base FHIR standard does not have (e.g., PWD registration, PSGC address parts).
The link between a coded element and its value set. Strength: required (only those codes), extensible, preferred or example (illustration only).
A value the profile requires exactly (e.g., ServiceRequest.intent = order).
A link from one resource to another (e.g., ServiceRequest.subject → Patient).
A Bundle is a package of resources. A transaction Bundle is processed all-or-nothing: either every entry is saved or none.

glossary.term: Interaction (create, read, update, search; POST, PUT, GET)
glossary.meaning: The operations a system performs on a FHIR server: create (HTTP POST), update (HTTP PUT), read / search (HTTP GET).
A create or update that first searches for an existing match (e.g., Patient by PhilSys number) so that no duplicate is made.
An identifier assigned by the business process (e.g., a referral number), used to recognise the same referral across systems.
Sending the same referral more than once leaves the same single result on the server.
Ways the receiving EMR learns of new referrals: asking the server regularly (polling), registering to be told (subscription), or receiving a message from the IOL (notification).
The data sent to the server (request), what the server sends back (response), and the content they carry (payload).
The server's reply code: 2xx = success (200 OK, 201 Created); 4xx = request error; 401 = not authenticated; 403 = not allowed.
The FHIR resource a server returns to explain errors or warnings (e.g., why a submission was rejected).
A FHIR resource (or equivalent document) listing which resources and interactions a system supports (L1-03).
A FHIR operation that checks a resource against its profile and reports errors.
A terminology-server operation that lists all codes of a value set.
A terminology-server operation that checks whether one code belongs to a value set or code system.
Output of the official HL7 FHIR validator or of Inferno (an open-source FHIR testing tool) showing errors found in submitted resources.
A server that holds code systems and value sets and answers $expand / $validate-code requests; the DOH HIE terminology server runs Ontoserver.
A commercial FHIR terminology server used for the DOH HIE terminology server.
Text formats for structured data; FHIR resources are sent as JSON (application/fhir+json) or XML.
The standard character encoding that supports all letters, including ñ.
The international date-time format, e.g., 2026-10-14T09:30:00+08:00.
Local time (UTC+8) / Coordinated Universal Time, the world reference time.
Uniform Resource Identifier / Locator — a text identifier or web address (e.g., an identifier system).
The URI that says which numbering scheme an identifier belongs to (e.g., http://philsys.gov.ph/fhir/Identifier/philsys-id).
Written directly into program code or screens instead of taken from the official source.
The kind of value an element holds (date, number, code, text).
Not in the correct format (e.g., an impossible date, letters in a number).
Part of a referral left on the server after a failed submission, without the rest of the referral.

glossary.term: Error path / negative test / exception scenario
glossary.meaning: A test that deliberately sends wrong or incomplete data or interrupts the exchange, to check the system fails safely.
Some parts of a submission succeed and others fail.
Holding a referral to send later (queue), sending again after failure (retry), and the documented manual alternative when the system cannot send (fallback).
A period when a server, service or network is unavailable.
A local copy of a code list or registry kept by the EMR (cache), refreshed at set times (scheduled sync).
A standard for launching apps inside an EMR with secure access to FHIR data (removed from Level 4 in Rev 6).
The table linking each data requirement to its FHIR profile, element, rules and the criteria that test it (Chapter 5).
A difference between this tool and the published IG that the TDG must resolve.
Row numbers in the TDG's eReferral data mapping (e.g., REF-15 Time Called).

glossary.meaning: The PHeReF profile names: "ERef" + the FHIR resource, i.e., the eReferral version of that resource with its Philippine rules.
The PH Core profile names, and the identifier slices for the PhilSys number and PhilHealth ID.
The example referral submission (transaction Bundle) published in the PHeReF IG; shows the expected interactions.
The person being referred: name, identifiers, birth date, sex, address, contacts.
A health worker as a person (name, licence).
A practitioner's role at a specific facility (e.g., doctor at Facility A); used as the requester and as the care navigator.
A health facility or network (name, NHFR code, address).
A relative or companion of the patient (next of kin / accompanying person).
The referral itself: what is requested, by whom, for whom, why, how urgent.
Tracks the referral workflow and its status (requested, received, accepted, rejected, completed).
A problem or diagnosis — chief complaint and working impression.
A measurement such as a vital sign.
A laboratory or imaging report, which can carry the attached result file.
Treatment given before referral — a medicine given / a procedure performed.
The visit at the referring facility during which the referral was made.
Who did what and when to a record — used for the professional signature and its date/time.
A FHIR resource for audit-log entries (one accepted way to store the audit trail).
A full list of codes from one source / the subset of codes allowed for a specific field.
An ID number of a resource (e.g., Patient.identifier = PhilSys / PhilHealth number; Organization.identifier = NHFR code).

glossary.meaning: Scrambling data while it travels over the network (in transit) / while stored on disks and backups (at rest), so others cannot read it.
Secure web connection (HTTPS) using Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.2 or 1.3 required). SSL and TLS 1.0 / 1.1 are older, insecure versions.
A digital document proving a server's identity, issued by a trusted certificate authority. Self-signed, expired or host-name-mismatched certificates are not accepted.
The set of encryption methods a TLS connection uses; forward secrecy (ECDHE / DHE key exchange) keeps past traffic safe even if a key is later stolen.
Strong modern encryption methods (AES-128 or AES-256).
Methods used for certificate keys (RSA ≥ 2048-bit, ECDSA ≥ P-256).
Weak or no-encryption methods that are not accepted.
Hash functions. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken; a single fast SHA-256 is not acceptable for passwords.
A one-way fingerprint of a password; "salted adaptive" means a random value is added and the calculation is deliberately slow (Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2) — TB-04.
Encryption keys must be stored separately from the data, e.g., in a key management service, a hardware security module (HSM) or a secrets vault.
Encrypting a whole disk (Windows BitLocker, Linux LUKS) or a database (transparent data encryption).
Proving who you are (log-in) / what you are allowed to do.
Multi-factor authentication — a second proof besides the password, such as a one-time password (OTP) by app, SMS or e-mail.

glossary.term: SSO / LDAP / Active Directory / OpenID Connect
glossary.meaning: Ways to sign in with one central account: single sign-on, directory services, and a web sign-in standard.

The limit of what a user may see or do — by role and by facility (TEC-09).
Discovering valid user names from different error messages; prevented by identical messages (TEC-09.1).
Blocking or slowing log-in after repeated failed attempts (TB-05).
Changing a record ID in a web address or API call to open someone else's record; must be blocked (TEC-09.3).
A user gaining rights they were not given (e.g., making themselves administrator) — must be impossible (TEC-09.4).
A logged-in period; a token is the digital pass that represents it. Idle sessions end after the time-out (TB-06).
Re-sending an old request or session to get access again; must be refused after log-out (TEC-10.1).
Removing a user's or system's access; deactivated accounts must lose access within the TB-12 limit.

glossary.term: System-to-system authentication (OAuth 2.0 client credentials, SMART Backend Services, mutual TLS, API key, JWT)
glossary.meaning: How the EMR proves its identity to the SHR without a person logging in; the method is issued by the SHR operator (TB-07). JWT = JSON Web Token, a signed digital pass.
Passwords, tokens and keys; must never appear in browser code, URLs, messages or logs.
Showing internal details in errors: a stack trace is a programming error dump; SQL is the database query language.
A record of who did what and when (TB-08); must be append-only — entries cannot be edited or deleted.
A security-relevant action such as a failed log-in, role change or account deactivation.
Security Information and Event Management — a central system that collects and analyses logs.
Network Time Protocol — keeps server clocks accurate so log times can be trusted.
Limiting the number of requests a client can make, to protect an internet-facing API (TEC-13).
An attacker secretly intercepting a connection; prevented by verifying certificates.
Making a service unavailable by flooding it with requests.

An automated scan for known weaknesses run with a valid log-in, so it can see more of the system.
The most serious weaknesses reported by a VAPT or scan.
This tool checks that defined controls work (black-box). It does not replace a VAPT or a full cybersecurity assessment.
Copies of data kept to recover from loss, and recovering them; system-only data = user accounts, roles, audit log and configuration that exist only in the EMR (TB-09, TEC-07).
Building privacy into the system and collecting / showing only the data needed by default (TB-11).
Collecting only what is needed / keeping it only as long as required / deleting it securely / removing identity from it.
The legal reason under the Data Privacy Act for processing personal data.
Data that identifies a person; sensitive personal information includes health data and government IDs (RA 10173).
Data Protection Officer / Privacy Impact Assessment — facility-level duties under the NPC rules, outside this tool.
A contract stating the service levels a vendor commits to (e.g., support response time); facility-level, outside this tool.
A contract governing exchange of personal data between parties; facility-level, outside this tool.
The computer or network address from which an action was done (recorded in the audit log).
User interface — the screens of the system.

entries.title: Encryption in transit — protocol & certificate
fields: TLS 1.2 or higher on every endpoint used for the eReferral (TLS 1.3 recommended). HTTPS only — plain HTTP disabled or redirected to HTTPS. Valid certificate from a trusted certificate authority (or the CA designated by the DOH for the sandbox), unexpired, host name matching.
Any web server or reverse proxy, API gateway, load balancer or cloud TLS termination; public or commercial certificates.
SSL 2.0 / 3.0, TLS 1.0 / 1.1; plain HTTP; expired, mismatched or self-signed certificates on endpoints used for exchange.
TLS scan of each endpoint (e.g., testssl.sh, nmap ssl-enum-ciphers, online TLS checker) — TEC-01.
NPC Circular 2023-06 §11, §16 (secure encrypted links); NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2; RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3)

entries.title: Encryption in transit — cipher suites & keys
fields: Forward-secret key exchange (ECDHE, or DHE ≥ 2048-bit) with authenticated encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). Certificate keys RSA ≥ 2048-bit or ECDSA ≥ P-256.
The "modern" or "intermediate" TLS configuration profiles of current servers and cloud services.
RC4, DES, 3DES, NULL, EXPORT or anonymous cipher suites; RSA keys < 2048-bit; MD5- or SHA-1-signed certificates.
Same TLS scan as TB-01 — TEC-01.

entries.title: Encryption at rest
fields: Personal and health data held by the system — database, stored files / attachments and backups — encrypted with AES-128 or stronger (AES-256 recommended). Encryption keys stored separately from the encrypted data and never hard-coded in source code. Exports containing personal data (e.g., CSV / Excel, L3-14) can be protected (encrypted or password-protected archive) when they must leave the system on removable media.

Full-disk / volume encryption (e.g., BitLocker, LUKS, cloud volume encryption); database transparent data encryption; file- or field-level encryption; encrypted backup tools. Keys in a key management service, HSM, OS key store or secrets vault.
Unencrypted database or backup files; keys stored with the data or in source code; home-made or proprietary ciphers.
Any one accepted evidence option (Instructions 4B): view-only demonstration, configuration screenshot with keys masked, cloud-provider / independent certification, or signed attestation — TEC-08.
RA 10173 §20; NPC Circular 2023-06 §11 and §25 (files on removable / portable media must be encrypted); NIST SP 800-111

entries.title: Password storage
fields: Passwords stored only as salted hashes using an adaptive algorithm: Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with a work factor per current OWASP guidance.
Framework password hashers configured with one of these algorithms; or authentication delegated to an external identity provider that meets this baseline.
Plain text; reversible encryption; unsalted or fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, single-pass SHA-256).
Stored form of one TEST password shown view-only, or a signed attestation naming the algorithm with the framework configuration — TEC-08.
NPC Circular 2023-06 §11 (password strength, password policy); OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet; NIST SP 800-63B

entries.title: User authentication
fields: One account per user. Minimum password length 8 characters (12 or more recommended). Lock-out or throttling after no more than 10 consecutive failed log-in attempts. Default / vendor passwords must be changed at installation. Online access to patient data (sensitive personal information) uses a secure authentication mechanism — multi-factor authentication, or log-in only over encrypted links (TB-01) — and user rights are managed in the system's user-management tool. Multi-factor authentication recommended for administrator and remote access.
Fixed standard (lock-out count: DOH policy default)
Local accounts, LDAP / Active Directory, single sign-on, OpenID Connect; authenticator apps or SMS / e-mail OTP for MFA.
Shared or generic accounts; default passwords left unchanged; unlimited log-in attempts.
TEC-02 tests (short password, repeated failed log-ins, account list).
NPC Circular 2023-06 §11, §13 (access control, need-to-know), §16 (secure authentication, system management tool); NIST SP 800-63B

entries.title: Session time-out
fields: Idle sessions are logged out or locked (re-authentication required) after a period the facility can configure. Default: not more than 15 minutes.
Application session time-out, OS screen lock integrated with the application, SSO session policy.
No time-out; time-out that cannot be configured; default above the DOH value.

entries.title: System-to-system authentication (EMR ↔ SHR / terminology server)
fields: Use the authentication method issued by the HIE / SHR operator (DOH). Credentials and tokens are kept on the server side, never exposed in browser or mobile-app code, and sent only over TLS (TB-01).
Fixed standard (method set by the SHR operator)
OAuth 2.0 client credentials / SMART Backend Services, mutual TLS, or API keys — whichever the SHR operator issues.
Credentials embedded in client-side JavaScript or mobile apps; one credential shared by several facilities or vendors.
Validator reviews the connection set-up during TS1 / TS2 and records it in the Notes of TS1-T.01.
SHR / HIE connection guide (DOH); NPC Circular 2023-06 §20 (data sharing) when external registries / APIs (PSA, DSWD, PhilHealth) receive personal data

entries.title: Audit log content
fields: Each entry records: user ID, date and time (Philippine Standard Time, or UTC with offset, from a synchronised clock such as NTP), action, patient / record affected, and source (workstation or IP). Entries cannot be edited or deleted by ordinary users. Authentication attempts and security events are logged and kept LONGER than general system logs; logs are backed up and archived (TB-09). Retention per the facility's policy, and longer when an incident is under investigation.
Database audit table, append-only log files, FHIR AuditEvent, central log server / SIEM.
Logs editable by end users; entries without user or time; logging that can be switched off by end users.

entries.title: Backup & recovery of system-only data
fields: Automated backup of data held only in the system (user accounts / credentials, roles, audit trail, configuration) at least daily; backups encrypted (TB-03) and stored separately from the production system; restore demonstrated and the expected restoration time documented.
Database dumps or snapshots, cloud backup services, off-site or second-site copies.
Backups only on the same disk / server; unencrypted backups; restore never tested.
TEC-07: restore demonstration, dated restore-test record, or provider backup report + signed attestation.
NPC Circular 2023-06 §21 (business continuity: backup, restoration and remedial time); RA 10173 §20

entries.title: FHIR & data format
fields: HL7 FHIR R4 (4.0.1); JSON (application/fhir+json), XML only if the SHR also accepts it; UTF-8; dates / date-times in ISO 8601 with time zone where the IG requires dateTime; the PH Core and PHeReF IG versions announced by the DOH for the test cycle.
Fixed standard (IG versions announced by DOH)
Any FHIR library, server or platform (open-source or commercial) or a custom implementation.
Proprietary formats in place of FHIR; resources that fail $validate.
HL7 FHIR R4; PH Core IG; PHeReF IG

entries.title: Privacy-by-design & privacy-by-default
fields: By default only the data needed for the referral is collected and shown; functions without a lawful basis can be switched off; dashboards show de-identified, aggregated data (L3-11); the database is reachable only through the application and authorised administration tools (no shared database log-ins for users); the system supports configurable retention periods and secure deletion or anonymisation at the end of retention.
Role-based views and field visibility, configurable optional fields, scheduled purge / anonymisation jobs, documented disposal procedure.
Hidden or unnecessary data collection switched on by default; no way to delete or anonymise records at end of retention; end users given direct database access.
L1-05.5 documentation; L3-11 dashboard test; TEC-03 role test.
NPC Circular 2023-06 §7 and §8 (privacy-by-design / by-default, privacy engineering), §9 (retention), §12 (database access via authorised programs), §28–30 (disposal)

entries.title: Account revocation & session invalidation
fields: Log-out invalidates the session on the server. Expired sessions / tokens are refused. A deactivated account cannot start a new session immediately, and its active sessions end within 15 minutes (DOH policy default). Access tokens for users expire within the idle time-out (TB-06) or are refreshed only while the user is active.
Fixed standard (revocation window: DOH policy default 15 min)
Server-side session store, short-lived tokens with server-side revocation list, SSO / identity-provider session policies.
Log-out that only clears the browser; tokens that remain valid for days; deactivated users who keep working until their session ends naturally.
TEC-10 black-box test (log-out replay, expiry, deactivation).
NPC Circular 2023-06 §13; OWASP ASVS V3 (Session Management)

entries.title: Error handling & logging hygiene
fields: Users see generic error messages (no stack traces, SQL, file paths, server or library versions). Secrets (passwords, tokens, keys) are never written to messages or logs. Application / debug logs exclude full patient identifiers and clinical content unless required for the TB-08 audit log; debug logging is off in production.
Framework production error pages, structured logging with field masking, log redaction filters.
Stack traces or SQL shown to users; tokens in URLs or logs; full PhilHealth / PhilSys numbers in debug logs.
TEC-11 (error messages, client-side inspection, log sample or signed attestation); TS3-08.
RA 10173 §20; NPC Circular 2023-06 §12–13; OWASP ASVS V7

entries.title: Vulnerability management
fields: A vulnerability assessment and penetration test (VAPT) or an authenticated vulnerability scan of the product version (same major version) at least every 12 months and after each major release, by an independent party or a security team separate from the developers. Critical / high findings fixed before go-live or covered by a dated remediation plan accepted by the Technical Lead. Security patches for critical vulnerabilities in components applied within 30 days (DOH policy default).
Third-party VAPT firm, DICT / government CERT assessment, recognised scanning tools with authenticated scans, bug-bounty reports.
No assessment; assessment of a different product; open critical / high findings without a plan; scans older than 12 months.
TEC-14 document check (date, scope, independence, finding status).

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Using the testing criteria
chapters.html:
1.1 Purpose and scope

The workbook decides, level by level, whether an EMR SYSTEM — the product, as offered by its vendor or in-house developer — conforms to the national HL7 FHIR standards (PH Core and PHeReF Implementation Guides) and may be used in the Health Information Exchange (HIE) for electronic referral. Each level must be PASSED before the next one counts. Every score comes from evidence, not from the evaluator's opinion.

  • In scope: the EMR system and its vendor/developer — application and commitment, product documentation, and tested conformance on the DOH test environment (sandbox), using test facilities and fictional test data.

  • Out of scope: engagement and deployment at an actual health facility (contracts / SLA, privacy registration and impact assessments, data sharing agreements, ICT assets, connectivity, personnel, training). These are handled after the system passes.

  • Not a security assessment: the security checks of Level 2D are CONFORMANCE testing of defined controls. Passing it is not equivalent to passing a vulnerability assessment and penetration test (VAPT) or a full cybersecurity assessment; TEC-14 only checks that an independent assessment exists.

  • Test roles: "referring facility" and "receiving facility" are TEST facilities on the sandbox. The system is tested in both roles — sender (TS1) and receiver (TS2).

1.2 Process flow

Step What happens Level
1.0 Registration The vendor/developer submits the letter of application and the System Profile (sections A–B); the Administrator logs the application. 0
2.0 Assessment of submitted documents Validators review the product documentation. 1
3.0 Validation Scheduled testing on the sandbox, witnessed by Observers. Validators record results and evidence references and recommend the results to the Technical Lead. 2–4
4.0 Issuance of certificate On approval of the Technical Lead once Level 3 is PASSED and no critical item is Not Met (Level 4 is the maturity target). Certificate details are recorded in System Profile section D. See Chapter 7. —

1.3 The levels

Level / part What it proves Proposed pass mark
0 — Application & Commitment The vendor has formally applied, identified the system and named accountable contacts. 90%
1 — Product Documentation Process flows, user manual, supported FHIR interactions, architecture (integration level), security design, release management. 85%
2A — TS0 Terminology & Registries Coded values and identifiers come from official sources (gate inside Level 2 — test first). 85%
2B — TS1 Submission A referral reaches the SHR complete and correct, without duplicating the patient. 85%
2C — TS2 Retrieval The receiving facility finds, shows and updates the referral; every status is time-stamped. 85%
2D — Security, Reliability & Exception Handling Safeguards and access boundaries work when the system is used (TEC-), and wrong, duplicated or interrupted exchanges fail safely and recover (TS3-). 85%
3 — Reports & Dashboard Reports reproduce the known test referrals exactly under the Indicator Definitions (Chapter 6). 85%
4 — Advanced Core-track (back-referral, multi-tier chain — move to Level 2 when the IG models them) and Maturity items. 75%

1.4 How each criterion is scored

  • Binary: Met (100%) or Not Met (0%).

  • Count: each countable part is a sub-item (↳). Mark each sub-item Met / Not Met / Not Tested / N/A; Required, Achieved, Result, Score and Outstanding are calculated. Example: 8 of 10 audit actions logged (TEC-04) = 80%.

  • All-or-nothing: marked like Count, but scores 100% only when all sub-items are Met (e.g., L1-02 user manual).

  • Tier (L1-04 only): Fully integrated = 100%; Standalone – manual encoding = 50%; Not Met = 0%.

  • Critical (★ / "Yes"): must be Met. A ★ sub-item that is Not Met or N/A makes the whole criterion a critical failure, even though the other sub-items still give partial credit.

  • Not Tested counts as 0% and makes the sheet INCOMPLETE. N/A removes a non-critical item from the score; on a critical item it counts as Not Met. Always record the reason for N/A.

  • Weight: critical items 2, others 1, information-only items 0. Weights are fixed before any evaluation starts.

1.5 Pass rule

A level is PASSED only when ALL THREE hold: (a) every applicable item has been tested, (b) every critical item and every ★ sub-item is Met, and (c) the level score reaches the threshold on the Summary sheet. Level 2 passes only when all four parts (2A–2D) pass. A level shows LOCKED until the level before it passes; its score is still shown so testing can run in parallel. While the thresholds are PROPOSED, a positive result is marked PROVISIONAL.

1.6 Design neutrality and the Technical Baseline

  • Outcome, not design: criteria state WHAT must be achieved and how it is verified. Architecture, language, database, hosting, screen layout and integration method are the vendor's choice and are never scored.

  • Specific where it matters: measurable minimums (encryption, password storage, log-in protection, session time-out, system-to-system authentication, audit log, backup, FHIR format, revocation, logging hygiene, vulnerability management) are in the Technical Baseline (Chapter 3). Meeting or exceeding them with any product is a Met.

  • Equivalent control: a vendor using a different control it considers equal or stronger submits a justification with evidence together with the L1-05 document. The Technical Lead decides before testing starts and applies the decision to all applicants.

  • Named sources: each coded value and identifier must come from the source named in Chapter 4; vendors choose how to connect (live look-up, scheduled sync or cached copy), not which source to use.

  • FHIR mapping: every referral data element is traced to its profile, element, cardinality and binding in Chapter 5. Update Chapter 5 first whenever an IG version changes.

1.7 Evidence

  • Server-side evidence (Levels 2 and 4): any ONE of (a) the Interoperability Layer transaction log on the sandbox (e.g., OpenHIM), (b) an Inferno or official FHIR validator report, or (c) the raw FHIR request / response payload captured during the session. A value shown on screen does not prove it was sent.

  • Evidence reference: for each row, write in the Notes column what the result is based on — file or screenshot name, SHR resource ID (with version where relevant) and the IOL transaction ID if available. Keep the files in the Administrator's repository under the Application No.

  • Version traceability: record the version/build actually tested, the IG versions and the testing dates in System Profile sections C and D. If the build changes during testing, the affected levels are re-tested (Chapter 7).

  • Proprietary documents (L1-04, L1-05, TEC-07, TEC-08, TEC-11, TEC-14): the vendor chooses how to prove compliance — full document; redacted version plus signed attestation; independent certification or report; or a view-only presentation recorded as "sighted". Source code, keys, credentials and internal network details are never required.

  • Confidentiality: evidence is used only for this validation and handled under a confidentiality undertaking signed by the Regional Validation Team. Only fictional test data is used.

  • Black-box first: security and reliability outcomes are tested by using the system.

1.8 Test data

Section Content Used in
A — Test referral Standard fictional values entered at the referring EMR and compared at the receiving EMR. TS0, TS1, TS2
B — Reconciliation set 10 known referrals with auto-calculated expected report values. L3-03 to L3-16, L3-20.2
C — Level 3 edge cases 6 referrals pre-loaded by the DOH on the SHR with fixed timestamps in a separate reporting month (month boundary, late update, duplicate, cancelled, status change, filter case). L3-17 to L3-21
D — Error inputs Error, duplicate, outage and security inputs (TD-D01 to TD-D22) with expected results fixed in advance. Level 2D: TS3-, TEC-09, TEC-13

All data are synthetic. The same values are used for every vendor in a test cycle; replace the [bracketed] placeholders with the official dummy facilities and identifiers issued by the DOH before testing.

1.9 Who does what — Regional Validation Team

Role Responsibility
Technical Lead Supervises the evaluation, decides on equivalent controls, approves the validation results and the conformance decision.
Validators (2–3) From the DOH-CHD or partner agencies (e.g., PhilHealth, DICT). Conduct testing with the Validator's Guide, record results and evidence references, re-test corrected items, and recommend approval.
Administrator Processes the application, keeps the logbook and evidence repository, schedules sessions, invites Observers, facilitates signing of the certificate.
Observers (1–2) From an LGU, hospital, academic / research institution or other agency. Witness the validation; do not score.

1.10 Step by step

  1. Fill in the System Profile (sections A–C before testing; section D after).

  2. Prepare the Test Data sheet (Sections A–D) and confirm the DOH has loaded the Section C fixtures.

  3. Evaluate Level 0 → Level 4 in order; in Level 2 test TS0 first.

  4. For every row choose a Result, mark the sub-items, and write the evidence reference and any N/A reason in Notes.

  5. Review the Summary and the Outstanding column. Items needing compliance are listed automatically in section D of the Printed Evaluation Report; after the vendor corrects them, re-test the item (and the related level if the build changed) and update the result.

  6. Print the Printed Evaluation Report (A4) and sign the Sign-Off.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Technical Baseline (TB-01 to TB-14)
chapters.html:
The criteria test OUTCOMES and leave the design to the vendor. This sheet states, only where a measurable bar is needed (aligned with RA 10173 and NPC Circular 2023-06 on the Security of Personal Data), the MINIMUM that the outcome must meet. Any product, architecture, programming language, database or hosting that meets or exceeds the baseline is accepted; the examples are illustrations, not endorsements.

Values marked "DOH policy default" are set by the DOH before any evaluation begins and are applied equally to all systems. Decisions on equivalent controls are recorded by the Technical Lead in the Notes column of the related criterion.

For every concept tested in Level 2A (TS0), this sheet names the authority, the code system / value set / identifier to use, and where to retrieve or verify it. HOW the system retrieves it (live look-up, scheduled sync or cached copy) remains the vendor's choice; the values must match the named source. Do not depend on external public servers such as tx.fhir.org (Connectathon Issue #9).

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Certification & Revalidation — PROPOSED
chapters.html:
A certificate is issued on approval of the Technical Lead when Level 3 is PASSED and no critical item is Not Met (Printed Evaluation Report, section D). Certificate number, date of approval, validity and conditions are recorded in System Profile section D and printed in section E of the report. Values below take effect after DOH approval.

7.1 Change classes and revalidation scope

Change class Definition Examples Required action Re-test
Major change A change that alters how the system exchanges, codes or secures referral data, or its architecture tier (L1-04). New or changed FHIR resources, profiles or interactions; change of exchange method (e.g., from per-resource calls to transaction Bundle); new authentication method; move from built-in to separate eReferral module; new major version number; migration of database / hosting platform; change of PH Core / PHeReF IG major version. Full revalidation before the new version is used in the HIE. Levels 1–3 (Level 4 if previously claimed)
Minor change A functional change in the eReferral module that does not alter the exchange method or security design. New or changed screens or fields mapped to existing elements; report / dashboard changes; workflow changes; terminology value-set update applied by the vendor. Partial regression test within 60 days (DOH policy default); notice to the DOH before deployment with release notes (L1-06). Affected TS1 / TS2 criteria + all ★ critical items of the affected part + TS3 + affected Security items + affected Level 3 items
Patch A defect fix or security fix that does not change data elements, exchange or reports. Bug fixes, performance fixes, security patches, UI text corrections. Notice to the DOH with release notes within 30 days; spot check at the next scheduled revalidation or if a problem is reported. None (spot check of TS1-T.01 / T.02 optional)
IG / terminology update The DOH announces a new PH Core / PHeReF IG version, terminology release or registry release for the HIE. IG technical correction or minor version; new SNOMED CT / PSGC release; new value-set version. Minor / technical correction: vendor conforms within the transition period and submits a notice (re-test of affected TS0 items). IG major version: revalidation within the transition period. TS0 + affected TS1 / TS2 (minor); Levels 2–3 (major)

7.2 Validity, surveillance, suspension and revocation

Rule Policy
Certificate validity 2 years from the date of approval, or until the system version is replaced by a major change, or until the end of the transition period of the next IG major version — whichever comes first.
Transition period for new national standards 6 months from the DOH announcement of a new IG major version (or as set by the DOH). Previously certified systems keep their certificate during the transition period and must be revalidated before it ends.
Surveillance The DOH may spot-check a certified system in production (with facility consent) using fictional test data on the sandbox or the interoperability-layer logs.
Suspension (temporary) (1) An unresolved Critical finding reported in production for more than 30 days; (2) a security incident attributable to the product until the root cause is fixed; (3) failure to submit the required notice for a minor change or patch; (4) failure to complete revalidation within the transition period. Facilities are notified; existing referrals continue, new deployments stop.
Revocation (permanent) (1) Misrepresentation of the product, version or evidence; (2) persistent non-conformance after suspension (not corrected within 90 days); (3) deployment of an uncertified version presented as certified; (4) breach of the confidentiality or test-data undertaking (L0-04).
Re-application after revocation Full validation from Level 0 after 6 months.

7.3 Required certificate content

  • Certificate number and date of approval

  • Product name and exact version / build validated (System Profile A.2, A.3) — matching every test run used

  • Vendor / developer name (System Profile A.1) and applicant category

  • Implementation Guide versions validated against: PH Core and PHeReF (System Profile D.2, D.3)

  • Terminology / registry releases used (System Profile D.4)

  • Scope / use case: electronic referral — sender (TS1) and receiver (TS2) roles; deployment type

  • Validation level achieved (Summary) and date(s) of validation

  • Date(s) of testing (System Profile C.8–C.12)

  • Conditions, if any (open Minor findings accepted with conditions, with due dates)

  • Validity period / expiry date and the revalidation triggers above

  • Signature of the Technical Lead (approval) and reference to the Printed Evaluation Report

7.4 Certificate of Validation — proof of concept

Proof of concept. The Certificate of Validation in this tool, its design, wording, signatories, security features and verification process are a proof of concept for discussion. They do not represent the actual DOH certificate or its implementation, and a certificate printed from this tool has no official standing. The notice comes from notice in criteria/certificate.yaml.

The web scorecard prints the Certificate of Validation from Output › Certificate and checks it from Output › Verify a certificate. Every part of it is kept as text in the repository, so a change is proposed and reviewed like any criterion (✎ Edit on each page):

Part Source
Title, subtitle, statement, microtext, signatories and their designations, verification address and its label, proof-of-concept notice, default orientation; the DOH seal and any further logos printed after it (e.g. the government advocacy logo or this system's logo) criteria/certificate.yaml (image files under tool/img/)
Certificate fields (number, dates, signatory, supersedes, orientation, conditions) and the HL7 FHIR release criteria/profile.yaml (System Profile)
Issued, revoked and superseded certificates, with their validation records criteria/certificates-issued.yaml (register of issued certificates)
Generation, security emblem, verification page tool/cert.js (fingerprint also in scripts/common.py)

7.5 Generating a certificate

  1. Fill in the System Profile. The application details (vendor / developer, applicant category, product name, exact version / build), the versions tested (HL7 FHIR release, PH Core and PHeReF IG versions) and the Certificate section (certificate number, date of issuance, expiry date, signatory and their name; optionally supersedes, orientation and conditions). If the expiry date is left blank it is 2 years from the date of issuance (PROPOSED).
  2. Open Output › Certificate. The page checks what stands between the evaluation and a valid certificate: every detail filled in; valid dates; Levels 0 to 3 PASSED with no critical item open; pass thresholds approved; a released criteria version. While any item is open the certificate prints as a specimen, with SPECIMEN — NOT VALID across the page.
  3. Choose the orientation (landscape or portrait). The layout fits one A4 page in both: long details first close up the spacing, then shrink the title and product name, then all the text, and the page warns when even the smallest size does not fit.
  4. Record the certificate. The page computes the certificate fingerprint and shows the register entry to add, with the full validation record. The Administrator adds it to the register of issued certificates in one commit (or asks for it through a Certificate record issue). Until then the Verify page answers Not found.
  5. Print and sign. Print / save as PDF prints the certificate edge to edge on white. It is valid only with the signature of the signatory (the Head of KMITS or the DOH CHD Regional Director) and the official seal.

The certificate shows: the certificate number in the upper right corner; the product name and exact version / build; the statement; a ruled table with the certificate number, date of issuance and validity, the developer and applicant category, the versions validated against (HL7 FHIR release, PH Core and PHeReF IG) and the result of each sheet of Levels 2 to 4 (the score when passed, "--" when not yet passed); the security emblem with the verification site and the certificate fingerprint; the signatory; and, in the foot line, the testing criteria version, its commit and the level achieved.

7.6 Security features

Feature What it does How to check it
Certificate fingerprint The first 16 hexadecimal digits of SHA-256 over the certificate's details, its FHIR release and its Level 2 to 4 results. Any change to a printed detail gives a different fingerprint. The web scorecard and the check script compute it the same way, and the check fails when a register entry no longer matches its fingerprint. Type it on the Verify page with the certificate number.
Security emblem The QR code in front and the security rosette behind it, both drawn from the fingerprint, so neither can be moved from one certificate to another unnoticed. Compare it with the emblem the Verify page redraws.
QR code Opens the Verify page with the certificate number and fingerprint. QR error correction level L, the smallest code for the address, so its modules print large; the rosette behind it is kept faint enough not to disturb reading. Scan it: the address must be the official verification site printed beside it.
Tick ring 64 long and short ticks around the emblem spell the fingerprint's 64 bits, clockwise from the ▼ mark. Compare tick for tick with the Verify page.
Guilloche The lobed ring of the emblem (6 to 14 lobes, counted on the Verify page), the interlaced border band and the corner rosettes, all drawn from the fingerprint, so every certificate has its own pattern. Count the lobes; compare the pattern.
Microtext Very small text along the frame, including the certificate number. Read it with a magnifier: it blurs on photocopies and scans.
Register of issued certificates The authority for every certificate: an entry is added, revoked or superseded only by a reviewed commit, so the history of each certificate is kept. The Verify page answers from it.

The fingerprint is not a digital signature: the method is public, so anyone can compute a fingerprint and draw a matching emblem. What a forger cannot do is add an entry to the register; authenticity therefore comes from the register, and the security features make a paper that does not match its entry easy to spot.

7.7 Verifying a certificate

  1. Open the Verify page. Scan the QR code (check that the address is the verification site printed on the certificate; a certificate printed from a release points to the draft scorecard, where the register keeps growing, and one printed from a draft or branch preview points to that build), or open Output › Verify a certificate on the official site you know and type the certificate number and the certificate fingerprint.
  2. Read the answer. Valid (recorded and within its validity period), Expired, Superseded (replaced by a later certificate, which is named), Revoked (with the reason), Not found (not in the register: issued after this version of the page, or not genuine), Fingerprint does not match (the paper or the code was altered, or the fingerprint mistyped) or Register entry inconsistent.
  3. Compare every detail shown with the paper: product, exact version / build, vendor, dates, versions validated against, results, signatory. A difference means the paper was altered.
  4. Compare the security emblem with the one the page redraws: scan the code; the ticks clockwise from the ▼ mark; the number of lobes; the slant of the faint lines.
  5. Check the microtext with a magnifier.

The page also shows the validation record: the evaluation details, the status of each level and the result of every sheet. For a valid certificate it offers a register copy: the certificate printed again from its register entry, in either orientation, marked REGISTER COPY — NOT VALID WITHOUT SIGNATURE AND SEAL. It serves as a reference copy; only the signed and sealed original is the certificate.

7.8 Register of issued certificates

criteria/certificates-issued.yaml lists every issued certificate. Each change is one commit, so the history of every certificate is kept in the repository:

Event Change Commit message
Issue Add the entry shown on Output › Certificate (or ask through a Certificate record issue) cert: record <number>
Revoke Set status: revoked and add reason cert: revoke <number> (<reference>)
Re-issue after a re-evaluation Record the new certificate with supersedes: <old number> cert: record <new number>

An entry holds the printed details, the FHIR release and the Level 2 to 4 results (covered by the fingerprint), the fingerprint, the status and the validation record: the evaluation details (application number, evaluation type, date(s) of testing, deployment model, terminology release, conducting office, signatory's designation, conditions), the status of every level, and for every sheet of Levels 0 to 4 its score, pass mark, status, criterion counts (met, partial, not met, N/A, not tested, info only), critical items not met and the criteria still needing compliance. The validation record is the benchmark of the system; it is not printed and not part of the fingerprint, and the check script makes sure its counts add up and match the printed results.

Never edit the details of a recorded entry: the check fails when they no longer match the fingerprint. Issue a new certificate that supersedes it instead.

7.9 Sample certificate for reviewers

The register holds one sample certificate, SAMPLE-2026-0001 (marked sample: true), with fictional data. It was never issued. Reviewers can use it to try the process end to end: open Output › Verify a certificate, choose verify it next to the sample (or type the number and its fingerprint), read the answer and the validation record, compare the security emblem, and print the register copy, which is marked SAMPLE — NOT A REAL CERTIFICATE. The sample is generated by the same code as a real certificate, so its fingerprint and validation record pass the same checks.

help.title: Form help
help.source: Instructions sheet of the scorecard workbook and the Technical Reference Guide (legacy Rev 9)

result.label: Result
result.help: Record what the evidence shows. Not Tested blocks the level; always write the evidence reference, and the reason for N/A, in the notes.

answers.Met: The evidence shows the requirement is fully satisfied.
answers.Not Met: The evidence is missing or does not satisfy the requirement. A Not Met critical item stops the level from passing.
answers.Not Tested: Not evaluated yet. Any Not Tested item keeps the sheet INCOMPLETE.
answers.N/A: Does not apply to this system. On a critical item, N/A counts as Not Met. Record the reason in the notes.
answers.Fully integrated: eReferral is part of the EMR, or a separate system that receives patient details automatically from it (score 100%).
answers.Standalone - manual encoding: Patient details are re-typed or copy-pasted into a separate eReferral system (score 50%).

binary.label: Binary
binary.help: Choose Met or Not Met for the criterion as a whole.

count.label: Count
count.help: Mark every ↳ sub-item. The score is the share of applicable sub-items that are Met.

all-or-nothing.label: All-or-nothing
all-or-nothing.help: Mark every ↳ sub-item. The score is 100% only when every applicable sub-item is Met; otherwise 0%.

tier.label: Tier
tier.help: Choose the integration level. Fully integrated scores 100%, standalone with manual encoding 50%.

yes.label: Critical
yes.help: Must be Met for the level to pass, whatever the score. N/A on a critical item counts as Not Met.

subs.label: Critical sub-items
subs.help: The criterion is critical through its ★ sub-items. Any ★ sub-item that is Not Met or N/A makes the criterion a critical failure.

no.label: Not critical
no.help: Counts toward the score with its weight, but a Not Met result alone does not stop the level.

weight.label: Weight
weight.help: How much the criterion counts toward the sheet score in %percent. [Criteria Score]x[Weight]=Weighted Score

validation_role.label: Validation role
validation_role.help: Who verifies the item criteria. Level 2 and Level 4 items must be confirmed with server-side evidence, not the EMR screen alone.

notes.label: Evidence reference / notes
notes.help: Write where the evidence is (file name, log reference, screenshot number) and the reason for any N/A.

status.PASSED: Every applicable item tested, every critical item and ★ sub-item Met, and the score reaches the threshold.
status.NOT PASSED: Tested, but a critical item or ★ sub-item is not Met, or the score is below the threshold.
status.INCOMPLETE: At least one item is still Not Tested.
status.LOCKED: The level before this one has not passed yet. Each level is a gate.

sheet.label: How to evaluate this sheet
sheet.help: Choose a result for every criterion, or for every ↳ sub-item of count and all-or-nothing criteria. The sheet passes when nothing is left Not Tested, every critical item and ★ sub-item is Met, and the score reaches the pass threshold. Write the evidence reference in the notes of each criterion.

threshold.label: Pass threshold
threshold.help: Minimum score for the level, set by DOH policy (scoring.yaml). PROPOSED until approved by the TWG.

conformant.label: Conformant for use in the HIE
conformant.help: Levels 0 to 3 passed and no critical item Not Met. Level 4 is the maturity target.

progress.label: Evaluation progress
progress.help: Share of items already evaluated (not Not Tested).
